cards.name: BASS-II
cards.full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
cards.fuel: Solids: acrylic (PMMA) films, sheets, rods and a sphere section; SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric
cards.flow: Fan-driven duct; 0-55 cm/s in the report's rod tests (the metadata says up to 40 cm/s); concurrent and opposed flow

outcome.text: Flames always went out when the fan was turned off (at cabin oxygen or lower); materials burned at lower oxygen than on Earth; authors warn fan-off may not work in high-oxygen, low-pressure or partial-gravity atmospheres

evidence.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) overview (BASS, BASS-II, BASS-M)
evidence.quote: BASS-II tests produced data on how ambient oxygen, ventilation, and fuel affect combustion and burning.

evidence.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) overview (BASS, BASS-II, BASS-M)
evidence.quote: With data from microgravity, scientists determined thin and thick fuel spread rates and a formula for transition from thin to thick fuels. Models predict higher spread rates than observed, so need improvement.

evidence.source: Olson S, Ferkul P, Fernandez-Pello C, Miller F, Wichman I, Bhattacharjee S, T'ien J. Flammability Limits from BASS-II Testing in Microgravity Compared to Normal Gravity Limits. 49th ICES, 2019.
evidence.quote: At the other extreme, the flames always quenched when the fan was turned off.

evidence.source: Olson S, Ferkul P, Fernandez-Pello C, Miller F, Wichman I, Bhattacharjee S, T'ien J. Flammability Limits from BASS-II Testing in Microgravity Compared to Normal Gravity Limits. 49th ICES, 2019.
evidence.quote: Flame extinctions occurred under conditions indicating that materials can burn at a lower oxygen concentration in microgravity compared to normal gravity.

airflow_off.text: In the PSI table, 17 tests record the flame going out as the airflow was turned down (at 14.8-20.9% oxygen) and 7 record it blowing out when the airflow was turned up. From its own rod tests, the report finds that at low airflow, the slower the airflow, the more oxygen a flame needs to survive. It also cites an earlier space experiment (its Ref. 11) in which flames spread steadily over thin fuels with no airflow at all at higher oxygen levels.

evidence.source: NASA PSI-25 (BASS-II) experiment table
evidence.quote: Bhattacharjee,B14,7/2/2014,183,174m,1 cm wide 200 micron thick PMMA,2,pot 0.9   0.5 and down,5  3  2   ext,250,44,15,none,0,none,0.2,none

evidence.source: NASA PSI-25 (BASS-II) experiment table
NASA PSI-25 (BASS-II) experiment table
Olson SL, Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Miller FJ, Fernandez-Pello C, Link S, T'ien JS, Wichman I. Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report. NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021.
evidence.quote: Last image is just before extinction as flow is turned off.

airflow_off.our_note: Our reading, not the report's: Moon Base air (30%+ oxygen) is richer than anything BASS-II tested (22.2% max), so a flame there may survive at airflows that would starve it in station air. BASS-II supports 'fans off' up to about 21% oxygen; it can't confirm it for Moon Base conditions.

goldilocks_flow.text: A band of gentle airflow, typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces, let PMMA burn at lower oxygen in microgravity than on Earth: the burn/no-burn boundary fitted to the flight data bottoms out at about 13.5% oxygen, below the 15.4% upward-burning limit from a normal-gravity study the report cites (its Ref. 23)

evidence.source: Olson SL, Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Miller FJ, Fernandez-Pello C, Link S, T'ien JS, Wichman I. Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report. NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021.
evidence.quote: The minimum O2 concentration of 13.5 percent O2 at a of 8 to 12 s–1 is significantly lower than the observed upward flame spread limit of 15.4 percent O2

evidence.source: Olson SL, Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Miller FJ, Fernandez-Pello C, Link S, T'ien JS, Wichman I. Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report. NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021.
evidence.quote: indicating the material remains flammable under the weak ventilation only obtainable in microgravity.

evidence.source: Olson SL, Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Miller FJ, Fernandez-Pello C, Link S, T'ien JS, Wichman I. Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report. NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021.
evidence.quote: This “Goldilocks” zone of flow is unfortunately typical of spacecraft ventilation flows near surfaces.

evidence.source: Olson SL, Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Miller FJ, Fernandez-Pello C, Link S, T'ien JS, Wichman I. Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report. NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021.
evidence.quote: at approximately 13.5 percent O2, in good agreement with the predicted a at the minima in the flammability boundary

context.text: Why it matters (Decadal Survey, quoted in the BASS-II poster)

evidence.source: Ferkul PV, Bhattacharjee S, Fernandez-Pello C, Miller F, Olson SL, Takahashi F, T'ien JS. Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment. ASGSR poster, 2014.
evidence.quote: Present tests, performed in normal gravity, are not adequate for reduced gravity scenarios.

Airflow range differs inside the BASS-II poster: 'up to 40 cm/s' (Approach) vs. '0 to 55 cm/s' (Hardware)

cards.name: FLEX
cards.fuel: Liquid fuel droplets, methanol and heptane, 2 to 5 mm
cards.gravity: microgravity (ISS, Combustion Integrated Rack, MDCA droplet apparatus)
cards.flow: Still air around a free-floating or tethered droplet
cards.atmosphere: Oxygen 10 to 50% (mole fraction 0.10-0.50), 0.5 to 1.0 atm (7.3-14.7 psi); nitrogen diluent; CO2 and helium suppressants
cards.varied: Oxygen, diluent, suppressant type and amount, pressure, fuel, droplet size
cards.moon_base_coverage: edge of the zone: 17 tests at 30-34% oxygen and 10.3-10.5 psi (just above the 10.2 psi limit); none strictly inside

outcome.text: Near Moon Base conditions (30-34% oxygen, 10.3-10.5 psi, still air), none of 17 droplet flames went out on their own: 15 broke apart and 2 burned to completion. Methanol kept burning down to about 12-13% oxygen.

evidence.source: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) overview (FLEX, FLEX-2, FLEX-2J, FLEX-ICE-GA)
evidence.quote: At high oxygen concentrations, however, the chemical times are small enough (relative to the characteristic flow times) such that the droplets will burn to completion rather than exhibiting flame extinction.

evidence.source: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) overview (FLEX, FLEX-2, FLEX-2J, FLEX-ICE-GA)
evidence.quote: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) experiment was designed to assess and quantify the effectiveness of inert-gas suppressants in microgravity and obtain the most conservative estimate of the limiting oxygen index for steady combustion.

evidence.source: Nayagam V, Dietrich DL, Hicks MC, Williams FA. Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity. 8th U.S. National Combustion Meeting, 2013.
evidence.quote: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

evidence.source: Dietrich DL, Ferkul PV, Bryg VM, Nayagam MV, Hicks MC, Williams FA, Dryer FL, Shaw BD, Choi MY, Avedisian CT. Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011. NASA/TP-2015-216046.
evidence.quote: As testing progressed, however, the science team noticed a propensity for the droplets to burn disruptively and not exhibit flame extinction (at a finite-sized droplet diameter).

context.text: NASA archived the data without interpreting it

evidence.source: Dietrich DL, Ferkul PV, Bryg VM, Nayagam MV, Hicks MC, Williams FA, Dryer FL, Shaw BD, Choi MY, Avedisian CT. Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011. NASA/TP-2015-216046.
evidence.quote: These extensive experimental results are not interpreted here; the intent is merely to make the data readily available for future scientific interpretation.

caveats: Ranges written as plans ('will vary'); confirm tested conditions in the PSI data
Overview has unfilled placeholders
Some 2009-2010 tests used fuel needles with a coating that contaminated the fuel; the report says disruptive burning may be due to it
The PSI table matches the FLEX paper value for value for all 274 of its tests; FLEX-216 (N03H201) and FLEX-230 (H01H103) appear only in the paper
PSI test numbers differ from the paper's FLEX numbers for 119 tests, so tests were matched by FLEX identifier
The PSI column headings lost their subscripts and superscripts: 'O', 'N' and 'CO' for O2, N2 and CO2, and a burning-rate unit of 'mm' (should be mm²/s)
The PSI file uses a legacy Windows encoding; a dash marks missing values
The PSI table repeats the paper's errors, such as test 114's pressure of 0

For tests 162-165 (Dec. 28, 2010) the report's Table VIII and Table IX disagree on CO2 (0.298 vs 0.32) and N2 (0.549 vs 0.53-0.54), and on test 165's starting droplet size (2.69 vs 2.59 mm); oxygen agrees. Records use Table IX, which matches the PSI table. Found in the hand spot check (2026-11-15).

cards.name: SAME
cards.fuel: Smoke from heated Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate on a wick (30 samples)
cards.flow: Air drawn over the sample at 2-8 cm/s while it heated (the hardware's design range)
cards.varied: Material, sample temperature, airflow, and smoke aging time (10-1800 s)
cards.measured: Particle number, size and mass statistics from three instruments; ISS and Shuttle smoke detector signals; particle samples for the microscope
cards.moon_base_coverage: none: smoke from heating without flame, in the ISS glovebox; no Moon Base atmosphere

outcome.text: Most smoke particles were smaller than 500 nm. Teflon and Kapton smoke was very fine and hard for light-scattering detectors to see; silicone and lamp-wick smoke carried much of its mass in particles over 1 micron. Holding the smoke (as if it leaked from a closed box) made particles grow. The Shuttle's ionization detector picked up every test.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: The small diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: The aging results show substantial increase in the average particle sizes

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: fire sensors must consider large particles in addition to the smaller particles seen with Kapton.

smoke_transport.text: A computer model of the station's US Lab found smoke spreads by air mixing instead of rising to the ceiling, so detection can take a long time and depends on where the source is and what equipment is in the way. In some low-smoke cases a detector never alarmed in the 300 s simulated. The model used the station's normal ventilation.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: This scenario is substantially different from that seen in normal gravity where the smoke concentrates near the ceiling and mixing is generally not as complete as seen in Fig. 6.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions.

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: The smoke source was activated 30 seconds after the simulation was initiated and the simulations were run for an additional 300 seconds.

smoke_transport.our_note: Our note, not the source's: with no rising smoke, the ventilation is what carries smoke to detectors. This model kept the fans on; it does not show how detection changes when they are off.

size_vs_earth.text: Smoke made in low gravity was typically 50% larger (count mean diameter) than under similar conditions on Earth

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than similar conditions in normal gravity.

recommendation.text: Future detectors should sort particles by size, or measure more than one size statistic, to catch both fine and coarse smoke while ignoring dust

evidence.source: Urban DL, Ruff GA, Sheredy W. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) final science report, March 2010, with four conference papers attached (Appendices B-E).
evidence.quote: Two possible effective means of achieving this size discrimination are to employ a detector that measures more than one moment of the size distribution or to use a detector that can classify the particles into size ranges.

caveats: The PSI table does not match the flight log: it lists four Teflon conditions (5 or 10 cm/s airflow, 1 or 2 mg/min weight loss, 1 or 20 min aging) and 'same conditions as 1-4' for the other materials, while the log has 47 test points on 30 samples and the results are for no aging and 720 s aging
The PSI table lists 10 cm/s, above the hardware's design range of 2-8 cm/s
The metadata describes an 'igniter' and a 'combustion event', but the report says samples were heated below the ignition point (smoke, no flame)
The metadata lists the hardware as 'Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware', which is the earlier Shuttle experiment (CSD)
The report's text calls 189 nm the silicone 'CMD' (count mean diameter), but its Table 1 lists 189 nm as the geometric mean; the count (arithmetic) mean is 257 nm
The 2008 paper in Appendix E says sizes were all below 300 nm; that fits the unaged results, but aged lamp-wick and silicone smoke in the final table averaged 308 and 422 nm

SAME and SAME-R disagree for some materials: SAME's count mean sizes are 1.5-2.4 times SAME-R's for Teflon and Kapton smoke and for unaged lamp-wick smoke, while aged lamp-wick and silicone smoke agree within 5% (unaged silicone within 16%). SAME-R later found the same heater setting could heat samples up to 30 C differently, which may explain some of the spread
The microscope grids came back contaminated with stray particles
The reference material (DBP) has no row in the results table
Flight log: one Kapton run was aborted and finished by hand, one missed the start of heating, and one record time reads '39:99'

cards.name: DAFT
cards.full_name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT / DAFT-2)
cards.fuel: No fire: background dust and test particles in ISS cabin air
cards.moon_base_coverage: not stated

outcome.text: First measurement of particles in ISS air: about ten times cleaner than a typical lab or office, thanks to HEPA filters. Pulling Velcro apart near the sampler sent counts above 30,000 particles per cc. The particle counter worked in microgravity, clearing the way for SAME.

evidence.source: Urban D, Ruff G, Sheredy W, Funk G, Funk N, Yuan ZG. Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) final report, 24 June 2008.
evidence.quote: However, these tests did provide the first measurement of the particulate air quality on the ISS.

evidence.source: Urban D, Ruff G, Sheredy W, Funk G, Funk N, Yuan ZG. Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) final report, 24 June 2008.
evidence.quote: Overall, the readings from these instruments are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally be seen in a typical laboratory environment (~ 4,000 - 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.

evidence.source: Urban D, Ruff G, Sheredy W, Funk G, Funk N, Yuan ZG. Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) final report, 24 June 2008.
evidence.quote: levels in the US Lab atmosphere are very low, about a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions.

evidence.source: Urban D, Ruff G, Sheredy W, Funk G, Funk N, Yuan ZG. Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) final report, 24 June 2008.
evidence.quote: shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark (P-Trak has a maximum count of 500,000 pt/cc).

outcome.our_note: Our note: everyday activity like opening Velcro can make particle counts jump, which is why SAME recommends detectors that can tell dust from smoke.

context.text: DAFT was a quick test that the particle counter planned for SAME would work in microgravity, since it normally relies on gravity to recycle its alcohol

evidence.source: NASA PSI-47 ISA metadata (i_Investigation.txt): Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / DAFT-2
evidence.quote: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME).

evidence.source: Urban D, Ruff G, Sheredy W, Funk G, Funk N, Yuan ZG. Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) final report, 24 June 2008.
evidence.quote: The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity.

caveats: The PSI table lists 2 sessions (2005); the report also describes 2006 sessions, one aborted after hardware damage and one deferred
The report gives early ISS readings as '2 - 5 pt/cc' in one place and as almost ten times below a lab's 4,000-6,000 pt/cc in another
DAFT tested instruments with a reference dust, not smoke

cards.name: SPICE
cards.fuel: Gas jets: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene diluted with nitrogen (75% and 50%)
cards.flow: Air flowing alongside the fuel jet: 5.4-65 cm/s per the metadata (the table lists -5.92 to 85.28 cm/s)

outcome.text: In microgravity, faster airflow or a smaller burner let a flame grow longer before it released smoke. The thesis counts 52 smoke points; propane was the least sooty fuel and pure propylene the most.

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length.

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: The fuel sooting propensities in these flames are as follows: propane < ethylene < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene, however ethylene is less sooty than propane for the 0.76 mm burner.

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: # Smoke Points 6 6 20 13 7

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: All smoke point flames were attached to the burner, i.e., not lifted.

airflow_and_smoke.text: One explanation offered: more airflow brings more oxygen to burn up soot. On Earth the airflow effect was mixed, and the author says the link is more complicated than expected

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: The effect of coflow velocity could also be explained by increased O2 transport if soot oxidation downstream of the flame sheet is transport limited.

evidence.source: Dotson KT. Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames. M.S. thesis, University of Maryland, 2009.
evidence.quote: indicate that the relationship of smoke point to coflow velocity and nozzle diameter is more complicated than initially expected.

caveats: The PSI table has 469 rows including 34 exact duplicates (dropped); many flames appear twice with times written differently (colons vs dots) and slightly different values
Counts disagree: the metadata says 526 flames, the overview says 250 tests and more than 70 smoke points, the thesis counts 52 smoke points, and the table has 435 unique rows
Some co-flow speeds are impossible or out of range: 8 negative and 15 above the metadata's 65 cm/s maximum (up to 85.28)

outcome.text: With no airflow, flames in normal air (21% oxygen) went out by themselves within 40 s. The report concludes that at 26.5% oxygen and above flames were quasi-steady, and at 27% oxygen and 10.2 psia and at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psia (inside our Moon Base zone) flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. Not every flame did: one 27% test it shows (19056F1) went out by itself at 45 s, and very large or very small flames went out at their limits. The authors call it a profound result that a common plastic could burn steadily in these NASA-proposed atmospheres. Pressure mattered little; methane flames went out within a minute in every atmosphere.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: All flames ignited in normal atmosphere self-extinguished within 40 s.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: In contrast, oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above resulted in quasi-steady flames.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: Figure 6. Flame growth from ignition to self-extinction in test 19056F1. The conditions are ethylene/N2, Δhc = 24 kJ/g, 4.55 g/m2s, 27% O2, 10.2 psia, L = 0.66 kJ/g, extinction at 45 s.

airflow_off.text: BRE flames had no airflow at all. In normal air they went out on their own, as the 'fans off' strategy expects; at 26.5% oxygen and above they generally kept burning. The report notes that cutting ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires, yet these flames kept burning without it in the oxygen-rich atmospheres NASA is considering.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

evidence.source: NASA PSI-20 ISA metadata (i_Investigation.txt): ACME Burning Rate Emulator
evidence.quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft

recommendation.text: The authors suggest NASA use its cone-calorimeter flammability test (Test 2) more, since it measures the material properties that predict these flames

evidence.source: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022), 1 Feb. 2022 (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments, Burning Rate Emulator).
evidence.quote: they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

caveats: ACME overview was written before flight
The PSI table gives oxygen levels per test day but no pressures; only a few tests' full conditions appear in the report (figure captions), so only 3 BRE tests are in tests.csv
PSI table date errors: 'Oct 17, 2020' is Sept 17 (test day 20261) and 'Dec 5, 2020' is Oct 5 (20279), per the report's log
PSI table oxygen typos: '3400%' (March 7, 2019) and '2100%' (April 1, 2019), read as 34% and 21%
The authors call the results preliminary
BRE burns gas through a burner to imitate solids; it is an emulation, not a burning material
Test 19070D1's heat of combustion is 24 kJ/g in one caption and 22 kJ/g in the next
The metadata's approach section is written as a proposal

Not every elevated-oxygen flame kept burning: test 19056F1 at 27% oxygen and 10.2 psia went out by itself at 45 s while still growing (Figure 6), an exception to the report's conclusion that 26.5% and above gave quasi-steady flames. The report doesn't explain the difference. Found in the hand spot check (2026-11-15).
The report never gives the pressure of its normal-air (21%) tests; it pairs 21% with 14.7 psia only in its list of NASA's candidate atmospheres. Found in the hand spot check (2026-11-15).
